# 2 Samuel Chapter 4 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 172r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_004_page_001.jpg

---

**1** When Ish-bosheth heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, he lost all nerve. All Israel was shaken.

**2** Ish-bosheth had two men who led raiding parties: Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, a Benjaminite town. (Beeroth is counted as part of Benjamin, **3** though the Beerothites had fled to Gittaim, where they have lived as resident foreigners ever since.)

**4** Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was lame in both feet. He was five years old when the news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths arrived from Jezreel. His nurse snatched him up and ran, but in her panic she dropped him, and he was crippled. His name was Mephibosheth.

**5** Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, went to the house of Ish-bosheth. They arrived in the heat of the day, while he was lying down for his afternoon rest. **6** They slipped inside as if collecting wheat, stabbed him in the belly, and escaped.

**7** They had entered the house while he was lying on his bed in his bedroom. After striking him down and killing him, they cut off his head. They carried it through the Arabah valley all night **8** and brought it to David in Hebron. "Here it is," they said to the king — "the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy who tried to kill you. Today the LORD has given my lord the king vengeance against Saul and his line."

**9** David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite: "As the LORD lives — the one who rescued me from every danger —

**10** when the man came to me in Ziklag claiming, 'Saul is dead!' — thinking he was bringing wonderful news — I grabbed him and had him executed. That was the reward I gave his 'good news.'

**11** How much worse when wicked men murder an innocent man in his own house, on his own bed! Should I not demand his blood from your hands and wipe you from the earth?"

**12** David gave the order to his men. They killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung the bodies by the pool in Hebron. As for the head of Ish-bosheth, they took it and buried it in Abner's tomb in Hebron.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — "lost all nerve":** Hebrew *raphū yadav* — "his hands went slack." This is not just worry; it is the collapse of a man who knows his only protector is gone. Without Abner, Ish-bosheth is a king with no army, no general, and no power.

**Verse 4 — The Mephibosheth insert:** The narrator pauses the assassination narrative to tell us about Jonathan's crippled son. This is not random. It answers the political question: even after Ish-bosheth's death, is there a Saulide heir who could challenge David? The answer is no — the last descendant is five years old and lame. The way to David's throne is open. But it also sets up the *hesed* that David will later show Mephibosheth in chapter 9.

**Verse 6 — "slipped inside as if collecting wheat":** The Hebrew is notoriously difficult here. The MT says they came "taking wheat" (*loqechey chittim*), suggesting a pretext for entering the house. The Greek Bible (Vaticanus) tells a different story: the doorkeeper fell asleep while sifting wheat. I follow the MT but simplify the awkward Hebrew into the practical sense — they used a ruse to get past the door.

**Verse 10 — "reward" and "good news":** David's speech is dripping with cold irony. The word *besorah* means "good news" — the same word that will later give us "gospel." The Amalekite of chapter 1 thought he was delivering the *besorah* of Saul's death. David's "reward" for this news was death. Now Rechab and Baanah have made the same catastrophic miscalculation. David's pattern is clear: anyone who kills the LORD's anointed — even David's enemies — will face justice, not reward.

**Verse 11 — "innocent man":** David calls Ish-bosheth *tsaddiq* — "righteous." This is remarkable. Ish-bosheth was David's political rival, the man who claimed the throne David was destined to hold. Yet David calls him righteous and demands blood-justice for his murder. David's theology of kingship is consistent: the LORD raises up and removes kings. Human violence against the anointed — or even the anointed's heirs — is not a shortcut to God's purposes.

*— PNEUMA*
